answers.stem_only: Two steps: move the instances into private subnets with no public IP addresses (they stay registered in the ALB target group, so the internet path is gone), and change the instance security group to allow HTTP only from the ALB's security group (security group reference) instead of 0.0.0.0/0. Not a NACL with ALB IPs (they change), not a VPC CIDR rule (too broad), and WAF does not attach to EC2 instances.

The default ALB health check uses path / and success code 200, so the 302 redirect makes every target fail; with all targets unhealthy the ALB fails open and still routes to all of them. Point the target group health check at the existing /health page, which returns 200 only when the application can serve requests. No application change, and not a TCP check (that would not show application state).

Security groups can be associated with a Network Load Balancer only when it is created; an NLB created without security groups cannot get one later. So create a new NLB with a security group, allow port 443 on the instances only from that security group, and move clients to the new load balancer. Private subnets alone with 0.0.0.0/0 would still allow any source that can route to the instances.

The client's TLS session must end on the instance, so the load balancer must not terminate TLS: use a Network Load Balancer with a TCP listener on port 443 (TLS passthrough) to a TCP target group, and let each instance decrypt with its own certificate and private key. An ALB HTTPS listener or an NLB TLS listener terminates the client session at the load balancer, even if it re-encrypts to the targets.
